questions.explanation: Air is matter: it takes up space, which is why the balloon swells, and it is made of particles, mostly nitrogen and oxygen, that each have mass. Blowing up the balloon packs in more of those particles, so the total mass goes up even though you cannot see what was added.
questions.misconception: Air is weightless “nothing” because it is invisible.

evidence.supports: Air is a mixture of mostly nitrogen and oxygen particles; all matter is made of particles.

questions.prompt: When a neon sign is switched off, its glass tube looks completely empty. Which observations are evidence that the tube still holds matter? Select all that apply.

A red neon glow whenever current flows, and extra mass compared with a pumped-out tube, both show particles are present. Not being able to see anything is not evidence of emptiness, because neon, like air, is an invisible gas. The red light itself is energy, not matter, but it takes matter inside the tube to give it off.
questions.misconception: If a container looks empty, there is nothing in it.
questions.hint: Pick the observations that show something is there, not ones that only describe what you can't see.

choices.text: The sealed tube has more mass than the same tube with all the gas pumped out.
choices.rationale: Evidence. Extra mass means extra matter, so the gas inside must be made of particles that have mass.

choices.text: You cannot see anything inside the tube.
choices.rationale: Not evidence. Neon and air are both invisible gases, so not seeing anything tells you nothing about whether the tube is empty.

choices.text: The tube's mass is the same whether the sign is on or off.
choices.rationale: Not evidence. A pumped-empty tube's mass would also stay the same when switched on, so this can't show gas is inside.

choices.text: The glass tube is sealed tight at both ends.
choices.rationale: Not evidence. A tube can be sealed whether it is full of gas or pumped empty.

questions.prompt: A diamond is clear and extremely hard. The graphite in a pencil is gray and soft. Chemists call both the element carbon. What decides which element a pure substance is?
questions.accessiblePrompt: A diamond is clear and extremely hard. The graphite in a pencil is gray and soft. Chemists call both the element carbon. What decides which element a pure substance is?
questions.explanation: An element is set by the kind of atom it is built from, not by its color, hardness, or state. Diamond and graphite differ in almost every way you can see or feel, yet both are built only of carbon atoms, so both are the element carbon. Later lessons explore how the same atoms can be arranged into such different materials.

choices.text: The kind of atom it is built from
choices.rationale: Correct. An element contains only one kind of atom, and that kind of atom names the element: diamond and graphite are both built of carbon atoms.

choices.text: Its color and shine
choices.rationale: Color cannot decide it: diamond is clear and graphite is gray, yet both are carbon.

choices.text: How hard or soft it is
choices.rationale: Hardness cannot decide it: diamond is extremely hard and graphite is soft, yet both are carbon.

choices.text: Whether it is a solid, liquid, or gas
choices.rationale: State cannot decide it: diamond, iron, and gold are all solids, yet they are three different elements.

questions.prompt: An STM's needle-thin probe sweeps across a surface without touching it. When the probe passes right over the top of an atom, how does the electric current compare with when it is over a gap between atoms?
questions.accessiblePrompt: A Scanning Tunneling Microscope, or STM, has a needle-thin probe that sweeps across a surface without touching it. When the probe passes right over the top of an atom, how does the electric current compare with when it is over a gap between atoms?
questions.explanation: The STM works a bit like reading braille with a fingertip. The current between probe and surface rises sharply as the distance shrinks, so bumps (atoms) and dips (gaps) show up as changes in current. A computer turns those changes into a map of the surface.
questions.misconception: Microscopes always work by bouncing light off an object.
questions.hint: What does the size of the STM's current depend on?

evidence.supports: Near an atom there is an electric current; farther away there is less, so current changes reveal atoms.

questions.prompt: A chemist in Brazil and a chemist in Japan speak different languages, yet both write “K” when they mean potassium. Why is that useful?
questions.accessiblePrompt: A chemist in Brazil and a chemist in Japan speak different languages, yet both write the letter K when they mean potassium. Why is that useful?
questions.explanation: Chemical symbols work like a worldwide alphabet for the elements. Because everyone uses the same symbols, a periodic table or a formula means the same thing in any language, and the short symbols also let a lot of information fit on one chart.
questions.misconception: Chemical symbols are abbreviations of English words, so they only work for English speakers.
questions.hint: What would go wrong if every country invented its own symbols?

evidence.locator: Section 5, Reading the Names of the Elements
evidence.supports: Scientists everywhere use the same chemical symbols to communicate about elements, whatever language they speak.

choices.text: Shared symbols let scientists everywhere identify elements the same way.
choices.rationale: Correct. A universal shorthand means a symbol means the same element in any language.

choices.text: K is short for the English word potassium, so everyone uses English.
choices.rationale: K does not come from the English name at all; it comes from another language, which is why it looks mysterious.

choices.text: Each country invents its own symbols, and K matches by chance.
choices.rationale: The symbols are shared on purpose, not matched by luck.

choices.text: Symbols only save ink; they don't carry a shared meaning.
choices.rationale: Saving space is a bonus, but the key benefit is that every scientist reads them the same way.

questions.prompt: On the periodic table, tellurium (127.6 Da) comes just before iodine (126.9 Da), even though tellurium is heavier. Which reason best fits how the table is organized?
questions.accessiblePrompt: On the periodic table, tellurium, 127.6 daltons, comes just before iodine, 126.9 daltons, even though tellurium is heavier. Which reason best fits how the table is organized?
questions.explanation: Columns are about shared properties. Tellurium behaves like selenium above it, and iodine behaves like chlorine and bromine above it, so the two swap places compared with strict mass order. Today's table is ordered by atomic number, the number of protons in each atom, which puts tellurium (52) before iodine (53) with no exception at all.
questions.misconception: The periodic table follows atomic mass with no exceptions.
questions.hint: Which matters more for choosing a column: an element's mass, or how it behaves?

questions.prompt: Using rounded atomic masses from the lesson, an oxygen atom is about 16 Da and a helium atom about 4 Da. How many helium atoms together have the same mass as three oxygen atoms? Give a whole number.
questions.accessiblePrompt: Using rounded atomic masses from the lesson, an oxygen atom is about 16 daltons and a helium atom about 4 daltons. How many helium atoms together have the same mass as three oxygen atoms? Give a whole number.
questions.explanation: Atomic masses let you compare atoms you could never weigh one at a time. Three oxygen atoms total about 48 Da, and each helium atom is about 4 Da, so it takes 12 helium atoms to match them.
questions.misconception: Atomic mass is just an ID number, not a measure of how much mass an atom has.
questions.hint: First find the total mass of the three oxygen atoms.

scope.section: 3. Classifying Elements; Key Science Concept: The Periodic Table of Elements

Helium 4.0 and oxygen 16.0.

evidence.supports: Atomic masses are given in daltons (unified atomic mass units), and table values are averages over isotopes.

questions.workedSolution: Step 1: 3 oxygen atoms × 16 Da = 48 Da. Step 2: 48 Da ÷ 4 Da per helium atom = 12 helium atoms. The spread's values (O 16.0 Da, He 4.0 Da) give the same answer: 48.0 ÷ 4.0 = 12.
